Hierarchical whole-body control · Unitree G1

System 1 (GR00T / ACT) → System 0 (SONIC): learning to speak SONIC's motion-token language

A high-level vision policy predicts SONIC's universal motion tokens from cameras. SONIC turns those tokens into balanced whole-body motor control. This page covers the architecture. It covers the open-loop evidence of what the policies actually learned. It covers how the work was validated and what comes next. The compact ACT hands-in policy emerges as the most practical System-1 policy to deploy.

RECOMMENDED. ACT (HANDS-IN)

At about 53M parameters ACT matches the 3B GR00T's latent-token accuracy. All policies land near 0.006 MSE. ACT also produces on-grid SONIC codes by construction. That means no FSQ-projection step and none of the projection-driven training instability GR00T's continuous head can show. It trains from scratch in-house. It is small enough to iterate on quickly. That makes it the most practical System-1 policy to plug into SONIC here. Its grasp-F1 comes in a bit lower than GR00T's. That gap is not visible in the sim rollouts. The two look comparable in practice. GR00T stays the stronger choice where broad generalization or language grounding matters. Part of ACT's edge reflects overfitting to this small three-task set.

03 · Learned action behavior (the open-loop evidence)

The clearest test of a behavior-cloning policy is whether it reproduces the demonstrated command. We replay each held-out episode's recorded camera observations through System 1. We overlay its predicted SONIC tokens on the ground-truth tokens the demonstration actually used. We compare the fine-tuned model against a near-zero-step base-proxy of the same model.

Per-task caveat. Cup and floor generalize well with normalized-MSE from 0.58 to 0.73. The bottle task is weaker at normMSE about 1.4. Only one training episode survives the held-out split for bottle. This is a data limitation and not a modeling one.

All four pass. ACT reaches the same 0.006 latent MSE as the 3B GR00T at about 1/60th the parameters. GR00T-A holds the best normalized-MSE at 0.87. The efficiency gap is what makes ACT the practical pick. It is not a raw-accuracy gap.

Trade-off. Efficiency vs grasp fidelity. ACT and GR00T land at essentially the same latent-token accuracy near 0.006 MSE. ACT hands-in even edges GR00T-B. So at about 1/60th the size ACT is the more efficient and marginally better choice overall. The one place GR00T leads is fidelity on sharp brief events. It scores higher grasp-F1 at right-hand 0.64 vs 0.39. It catches exact open and close timing a bit better than ACT's smaller discrete head. In the sim rollouts that gap was not heavily visible.

06 · Implementation in brief

SYSTEM 1 · ACT recommended

ACT baseline (~53M) that wins on efficiency

This is LeRobot's action-chunking transformer. It is a conditional VAE over a transformer with an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 encoder. It trains from scratch on the same data and split for a like-for-like comparison. Its L1 head is swapped for a 32-way discrete FSQ classifier over the 64 token dims. That makes it discrete by construction and it lands on SONIC's grid natively. The L1 head is kept for hands. It trains on a single-column copy of the dataset.

Net effect. SONIC-token accuracy is on par with the 3B GR00T at about 1/60th the size and with no projection step. It is the practical System-1 pick here.

SYSTEM 1 · GR00T

GR00T N1.7 fine-tune

This fine-tunes NVIDIA's GR00T N1.7 under the G1 embodiment. The SONIC latent tokens already exist in the dataset so no encoding step is needed. It consumes 3 cameras plus a 46-D state plus 1 language instruction. It uses 19 episodes with 3 held out. Training runs about 20k steps on 3 H100s with plain DDP and bf16. Latent and per-hand losses are logged separately.

This is the larger and more capable backbone. It is the better bet where broad generalization or language grounding is the goal.

HANDS

Hands-out vs hands-in

The 64-D latent is learned identically in both. Only the 14 hand dims differ. Hands-out zeroes them because varying hand DoFs are hard for SONIC. It is the clean baseline that tests the motion-token manifold without hand noise. Hands-in fills them and solves the multi-DoF mismatch. It uses per-task 0-to-1 normalization and task-conditioning and active-dim loss masking. It is the variant that learns real grasping.

INTEGRATION

Plugging into SONIC

Both models emit into SONIC's 64+14 universal token space. ACT is discrete by construction. GR00T's continuous prediction gets an FSQ projection onto the valid grid so every token is an executable code. SONIC then decodes it into real-time motor control.

INFERENCE-TIME

Receding-horizon stitching and reranking

Execute the first 1/5 of each 40-step chunk then replan. Blend overlaps for minimal jerk. Tokens are never interpolated directly. We switch to the newest chunk or blend in decoded-pose space. Best-of-N candidates are scored on smoothness plus a SONIC decoder round-trip. This cut discontinuity by up to two orders of magnitude. It trimmed latent error by 10 to 30 percent.

TOPReward · bootstrap RL

Advantage-weighted BC

An advantage-weighted BC pass using LeRobot's TOPReward. A frozen Qwen3-VL scores task progress from head-camera video. The effect is modest. It is data-side reweighting and not true rollouts. This sim has no task objects or task reward.

07 · What's next (given more time)

  • Folding tasks. The other 2 of the 5 tasks lack provided SONIC tokens. Encoding them is in progress to extend all policies to the full task set.
  • Closed-loop physics and video. A custom IsaacSim environment shows promising early tests with much cleaner lower-torso motion. It will produce the executed EE-error and stability and no-fall numbers. It will also produce higher-quality videos of the G1 executing the policy.
  • Scale ACT. Given its efficiency win the natural next step is to push the discrete-head recipe with a larger backbone and more data. This comes before reaching for the 3B model.
